t: the zav. A man from whose private organ there issues a discharge (a purulent emission due to illness) that makes him unclean (for the definition of a zav and the details of his laws see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah, chapters 2-3).
and the zavah and the niddah. A woman who sees blood that makes her unclean, whether she saw it in the days of niddah or in the days of zivah (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah, chapter 6).
and the woman who has given birth. Who is unclean like a niddah (ibid. 10:1).

and they defile a person through touching and carrying. If a clean person touched one of these four or carried one, even without touching, he becomes unclean; the same applies if he moved it, for one who moves is included in one who carries (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:6-7).

and they defile a bed, seat, and riding object beneath them and make them a father of uncleanness. These four defile vessels made for lying, sitting, or riding that are beneath them (even if they do not touch them), and these become a father of uncleanness (as explained below, chapters 6-7).
and they defile a shelf-load upon them. They defile all vessels carried on them with "madaf uncleanness", which is a light uncleanness (first degree of uncleanness; below 6:3).
a minor zavah. One who saw blood in the days of her zivah for only one or two days, and must keep one clean day for her purification ("shomeret yom keneged yom") and does not bring an offering.
a major zavah. One who saw blood for three consecutive days, and must count seven clean days and bring an offering when she is purified (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:7-8).

due to force. That she saw blood as the result of some act and not because of the body's natural cycle; even so the woman becomes unclean (ibid. 5:1; unlike a zav, who does not become a zav if he saw because of force, Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 2:2-5).
a zav with two sightings or with three. One who sees two sightings of discharge becomes a zav and defiles a bed and seat, and if he saw three he must also bring an offering (ibid. halachot 6-8).

a one-day-old girl becomes unclean as a niddah, a ten-day-old as a zavah. If she saw blood on the day of her birth, she becomes a niddah for seven days, and if she continued to see also in the three days after that, she becomes a major zavah (see also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 4:1, 11:2).
a girl three years and one day old. From this age onward a woman's intercourse is considered intercourse (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:13).
she defiles the one who has relations with her. The man who has relations with her becomes a father of uncleanness and defiles like her.
as will be explained. Below 3:1-3.
a one-day-old boy becomes unclean through zivah, and the same applies to converts and slaves, etc.. See also Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 3:6.
a eunuch by man and a eunuch by nature. A man whose sexual development is impaired, whether it was impaired by a person or he was born impaired (see Hilchot Ishut 2:13-14).
become unclean through zivah. Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah, there.

a woman does not become unclean through white. Through a white appearance. Even if it is thick like blood, since it does not have the appearance of blood, it does not defile (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 5:6).
nor a man through red. Through blood.
a tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and whose sex is unclear. [Note: In his Commentary on the Mishnah, Rambam vocalizes this word: "tumtom".]
and an androginos. One who has both male and female organs.

they are given the stringencies of a man and the stringencies of a woman... and their uncleanness is in doubt. Since there is doubt whether they are male or female (see Hilchot Ishut 2:24-25; see also Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 3:7).
therefore one does not burn terumah and sacred offerings on their account. One does not burn terumah and sacred offerings that became unclean through them.

and they are not liable on their account for the uncleanness of the Temple and its sacred offerings. Neither they nor one who became unclean through them is liable to karet if he entered the Temple or ate sacred offerings deliberately (see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:12, Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 18:13).
one burns on their account terumah and sacred offerings. Since there is uncleanness here in any case, whether they are male or female.

but they are not liable on their account for entering the Temple. And the same applies to their not being liable for eating sacred offerings (Or Sameach, and see Tosefta Zavim 2:2). Some wrote that they are liable to karet for eating sacred offerings (Minchat Chinuch 178:2).
as it says. Regarding sending the unclean out of the Temple.
the uncleanness of a definite male or the uncleanness of a definite female. In this case it is not known whether the uncleanness is due to a male or a female.

he touched it himself... he is liable for entering the Temple. The commentators had difficulty with the reason for this and tried to explain it in various ways (see Responsa Rema of Fano 130, Aruch HaShulchan 106:21 and others). Some wrote that the text here should read "exempt", as in the Tosefta according to the Rash (Rash, Zavim 2:1; see Chazon Nachum, Zavim 2:1, Meromei Sadeh of the Netziv, Niddah 28b).
they learned from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in interpreting the verses.
her flow. Her blood.
and we have already explained the matter of the prohibition of a niddah, etc.. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 5:7-10.
but if she saw green blood, it is clean. The woman does not become a niddah through it, and if the woman is already a niddah, green blood does not defile like niddah blood.

and it is not like her spittle and the other liquids that come out of her. Although the spittle of those who defile by lying and sitting, and other liquids that come out of their bodies, defile as a father of uncleanness (below, halachot 14-15), green blood does not defile like them (and later authorities disagreed whether it has the law of the liquids of a zav that defile as an offspring of uncleanness or the liquids of a zav that are entirely clean; see below halachah 16; Noda BiYehudah, second series, Yoreh De'ah 97; Aruch LaNer, Niddah 41b).
for spittle rolls up and comes out. It rolls into the shape of a drop and comes out of the body that way.
and this one oozes and goes down. Flows. Since it does not resemble spittle, it is not included among the liquids that come out of the body and defile as a father of uncleanness.
from her side. From her abdomen, by caesarean section.
and blood came out with it from the side. This refers to blood that came from the source (the womb) but exited through the abdominal wall (Noda BiYehudah, there; see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:5).

and the woman is clean until blood comes out of her through the womb. Although the blood defiles like the blood of a niddah and a woman who gave birth, the woman does not defile by lying and sitting as long as blood has not come out through the opening of the womb, and she also does not become unclean with the uncleanness of childbirth because the baby came out through the abdominal wall (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah, there).
the source of a woman that was uprooted and fell to the ground. A piece of the womb was uprooted and fell from it.

the woman is unclean with uncleanness until evening. Since the source is unclean, and when it was uprooted and fell it touched the woman's body and made her unclean, she requires immersion and is unclean until evening (Rashi, Niddah 41b).
that exuded like two drops of pearls. That two drops of blood, white and clear like the appearance of pearls, appeared from it.

the woman is unclean with uncleanness until evening. Since the drops touch the source and touch the woman as they come out of her (Rashi, there; Aruch HaShulchan 107:10 explained that things coming out of the source are not unclean, but the Torah decreed that the woman becomes unclean every time her source opens and something comes out of it).
for it is only from outside the source. Since it is not the way of the source to exude fewer than two drops, it is reasonable that this drop did not come from it.
it does not defile by carrying, and it is like semen. For semen does not defile by carrying (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 5:1).

whether from an adult man or from a minor, etc.. The first sighting of a zav defiles by touch like semen, even if it is a minor's, although a minor's semen does not defile until he is nine (ibid. halachah 2).
as we have explained in Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah. 2:6.

if he saw one extended sighting as two. If the discharge came out of him without interruption for a length of time that makes this sighting count as two sightings (the time "of immersion and drying"; see there halachah 10).
but the one who moves the last drop. Only the last drop counts as the second sighting of discharge, which defiles the one who moves it.
the first sighting of a leper. The first sighting of discharge of a leprous person.

for it says of spittle, "and if the zav spits on the clean". The verse continues, "he shall wash his clothes and bathe in water and be unclean until evening", and from this we learn that spittle is a father of uncleanness that defiles people and vessels.
drops of zivah. Drops of discharge.
as we have explained. Above, halachah 14.
like an offspring of uncleanness. Its uncleanness is light, and it does not defile people and vessels by Torah law.
his blow. His wound.

each of these is like unclean liquids that do not defile a person. These liquids are not considered a father of uncleanness; rather they have the law of liquids that touched a father of uncleanness and became first-degree uncleanness, and they do not defile a person.
but they defile vessels by rabbinic law. For the Sages decreed that all unclean liquids defile vessels.
as will be explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 7:1-2.
and putrid fluid. Pus (Commentary on the Mishnah, Machshirin 6:7).
and liquid stool. Liquid excrement.

like them from the rest of humanity. They have the law of these liquids coming out of all other people, and are clean, for these fluids are not considered a liquid, and therefore the Sages did not decree uncleanness on them like other liquids (see Hilchot Tum'at Ochalin 10:7).
his coughing and his sneezing, etc.. Fluids that come out of the body through spitting or as a result of coughing, a cold, and the like.
from the mouth of the organ. From the private organ.
he was sucking and spat blood. He has a wound in his mouth and sucks it and spits blood.
for the blood he sucks cannot be without drops of spittle. See also Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 4:23.
it defiles when wet and dry. Whether it is still moist or has dried.
but if it dried too much, it does not defile; and how long, etc.. See also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 5:14 (and see there 1:13, 3:11, 4:12 regarding a carcass and a creeping creature).
from time to time. For twenty-four hours.
and if the water was lukewarm at the start, etc.. The test is valid even if the water did not remain lukewarm for the entire soaking.
words of tradition. The tradition of the Sages.

flax that a niddah spun, the one who moves it is clean. It is the way of spinners of flax to moisten the thread with the spittle in their mouths, and when a niddah spun it, although the thread is saturated with her spittle, the one who moves it is not unclean since it has already dried.
and if it was wet. The flax.
the one who moves the cup is clean. Since the zav did not drink, his mouth remained dry and no spittle came out of it (Aruch HaShulchan 108:8).
because of the moisture of the zav's mouth. That clings to the wall of the cup.
the one who moves them is clean. For these foods are dry, and therefore the zav's spittle does not come out when he eats them.
the cucumber and the melon. Which contain liquids.
peels of beans and peels of lupines, etc.. Peels of types of legumes that people who eat them usually peel with their mouths, and the spittle clings to these peels.
as will be explained. Below, halachah 10.
in the marketplaces. Public places.
one follows the majority in them. If the majority of Jews in that place... the one who moves them is clean (as below, halachah 6).
if its appearance was nullified. That the appearance of the blood is not noticeable in the water.
if it was mixed with clean blood or with wine. Whose color does not change the appearance of the blood.

one views it as if it were water. One estimates the clean blood or the wine as if they were water; if there is enough of them to nullify the appearance of the unclean blood had they been water, it is clean (see also Hilchot Shechitah 14:6, Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 2:22).
if it was bound together as in its creation. For spittle is thicker than water, and the bubbles in it bind to each other so that it is noticeable in the water.
urine of one unclean from these. Urine of one of those who defile by lying and sitting.
it was mixed with the urine of gentiles. Clean urine mixed with the urine of gentiles, who defile like zavim.

one follows the majority. One does not follow the appearance here (viewing the urine as if it were water), since the uncleanness of gentiles as zavim is rabbinic, they were lenient with their urine, to nullify it by majority alone (Rash, Taharot 4:6; see Aruch HaShulchan 108:14-15, who rejected this interpretation of Rambam and explained otherwise).
a pit. A hole.
they ask for urine. Which they use for laundering.
and he laundered it. He washed it.
the liquids with which he laundered are unclean. Since the unclean urine is mixed with them.
whether he laundered it with urine. Of a clean person.
whose urine was uprooted. From its source, but it had not yet left her body.
at the end of the seven days of counting. A zavah must count seven days clean of blood, and on the seventh day she immerses and is clean if she saw no blood until evening.
and urinated. Passed water.
and converted and immersed and urinated after she immersed, it is in doubt, etc.. For a similar law regarding a gentile who converted see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 5:18.
slaves become unclean through zivah, etc.. As above 1:4.

so that a Jewish child will not become accustomed to a gentile for homosexual relations. Gentiles are suspected of homosexual relations, and therefore they decreed uncleanness on them so that people would keep away from them (for further distancing for this reason see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 22:5).
and less than this age their intercourse is not intercourse. See Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:13.
for if they were zavim by Torah law, their semen would be a father of uncleanness like the semen of a zav. As above 1:14.

lest they come to burn terumah and sacred offerings because of it. They should not burn the terumah and sacred offerings that became unclean through this uncleanness, since by Torah law they are entirely clean.
and their bed and their riding object. Items fit for lying or riding on which gentiles lay or rode (and the same applies to items fit for sitting on which gentiles sat; see below 6:1).
and one who has relations with a gentile woman. For one who has relations with a niddah or zavah becomes a father of uncleanness like her (below 3:1-3).
as we have explained. At the beginning of this halachah.

defiles when wet and does not defile when dry. Unlike the blood of a Jewish niddah, zavah, and woman who gave birth, which defiles wet and dry (above halachah 1); the Sages made this distinction to make known that the uncleanness of gentiles is rabbinic (as above regarding a gentile's semen; Commentary on the Mishnah, Niddah 4:3).
and defiles by moving. If he moved a clean item, it defiles it as zavim and their companions do (see below 8:1-2).
and defiles a bed and riding object like a niddah. It defiles items meant for lying or riding that are beneath him, although he does not touch them, just as a niddah defiles.
on which a niddah trod. She defiled it in one of the five ways in which a zav and his companions defile a bed and riding object, each of which is called a midras (for their details see below 7:1).
an offspring of uncleanness, like the vessels that he touches. Which are only first-degree uncleanness.
since it says "and her niddah shall be upon him", I would not know that he defiles a bed. Since he is unclean like her, it is clear that he will defile a bed just as she defiles.
from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in expounding the verse.

for Scripture removed it from severe uncleanness, etc.. The verse comes to take the man who has relations with a niddah out of the category of severe uncleanness like a niddah, and put him in the law of light uncleanness.
whether one who comes, etc.. One law applies to all of them, that one who has relations with them defiles like them.
one who keeps day for day. A zavah who saw blood for only one or two days and must keep one clean day for her purification (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:7-8).
whether in an unnatural way. Intercourse in the rectum, from behind.
the one who begins. The start of the act (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:10).
the one who completes. The completion of the act (see there).
whether an adult who had relations with a minor, etc.. Even when one of them is not subject to punishment.
but less than this he does not become unclean as one who has relations with a niddah. Since below this age their intercourse is not considered intercourse (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:13).
and likewise one who has relations with a zav. One who had relations with a zav (homosexual relations).
or one who was had relations with by a zav. A woman who had relations with a zav (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 1:4).
and a woman who gave birth, even if she did not see blood. She too is unclean in this case (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:1).

all of them become unclean retroactively, etc.. They defile the clean items they handled before they were found unclean, from the last day-and-night period or from the time of the last examination, as explained shortly.
and she has no set time (veset). Her cycle does not come at a fixed time, so she does not know when she will see blood and become unclean.
in the morning. In the early morning.
all the clean items she handled. Clean things she dealt with.
from the time of examination. From the time she last examined herself.
unclean retroactively. Since she has no set time, she may have become unclean immediately after the previous examination and not noticed until she saw now.
they are unclean retroactively up to twenty-four hours. If between one examination and the next more than a day and night has passed, the woman is not unclean retroactively beyond a day and night.

and the cloth after intercourse, etc.. It is the way of women to examine themselves after intercourse with a cloth (called an "ed"), in case they became unclean during intercourse (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 4:14-16).
because she does not examine with it well. Because of the haste before intercourse, the examination is not done properly.
her time is sufficient for her. She defiles only from the time she saw (see also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 9:4).

and she is presumed a niddah from the time of her set time. Even though more than a day and night has passed since the set time, since she has a fixed set time it is reasonable that she became unclean at the time of her set time.
at the time of her set time. At the fixed time of her seeing (see below, halachah 6).
she feels in herself. She knows that the blood is about to come, according to bodily events.
she feels the mouth of her belly and the lower part of her intestines. She feels heaviness in her lower abdomen.
she is seized by a chill. She feels heat and shivering.
and the like. See also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 8:2.
accustomed. Used to it.

one who sees a stain. Of blood on her flesh or her clothes; she is unclean by rabbinic law, lest it be from blood that came from the source (for the definition of a stain that defiles see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah, chapter 9).

until the time of examination. Even if the last examination was done more than twenty-four hours earlier, for in this matter a stain is more severe than a sighting, since there is a concern that it came out long ago (Rabbi Yom Tov Algazi, cited in Kesef Mishneh; and see the next paragraph).
and likewise the garment on which the stain was found is unclean retroactively. And the clean items that touched it during this time became unclean.
unclean from before the laundering. For the stain may have been there before the laundering and did not come out in the laundering.
and even if the stain was found moist. For it is reasonable to say that the blood came out of her body not long ago and has not yet dried.
and all the women whose time is sufficient for them. Women who are unclean retroactively only from the time they saw (see below 4:1; and see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 9:5).
their stain is like their sighting. The same law.
to defile a person and garments. For their bed and riding object are a father of uncleanness that defiles people and vessels.

and even an earthenware vessel enclosed with a tight cover, etc.. That has a tight, fitted cover. Although it does not become unclean in a tent of the dead (Hilchot Tum'at Met 21:1), it becomes unclean through the moving by a zav (see below 8:3).
but they do not render the man who had relations with them retroactively impure. See also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 8:13, 9:3.

only as one who touches. One who had relations with one of these women before they were found impure does not become retroactively impure with severe impurity, as one who has relations with a niddah, but is like a person who touched a niddah, who is a derivative of impurity and renders only food and drink impure.

one who has relations with her after the stain was found is impure as one who had relations with a niddah. For from the moment she saw a stain she is impure going forward and no longer has a presumption of purity, and therefore one who has relations with her becomes impure as one who had relations with a niddah (unlike the case of one who had relations retroactively, who does not become impure as one who had relations with a niddah, since at the time he had relations the woman was presumed pure; Ritva, Niddah 15a).
when a fetus put out its hand. Outside its mother's body.

its mother is impure as a woman who gave birth. For purposes of impurity she is considered as having given birth (although for the days of purity she is not considered as having given birth until most of the infant has emerged; see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:7).
that we have explained. Above halakhah 4.
and the impurity of regular cycles and the impurity of stains. Which are explained above halakhot 5-7.
we suspend. We leave the matter undecided.

unconsecrated food prepared in the purity of sacred food. Unconsecrated food whose purity people guard as if it were sacred food, which for some purposes is treated as sacred (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 12:16).
but those prepared in the purity of terumah. Although people guard their purity at the level of the purity of terumah, for this purpose they are not considered terumah.

and unconsecrated produce that is tevel for challah. Dough from which challah has not yet been separated. Although the challah itself is equal to terumah in its level of purity, this dough is considered unconsecrated and does not become impure with this impurity (ibid. 11:14-15).
that each of these women. Who became impure through one of the impurities mentioned at the beginning of the halakhah.

and one who has relations with a woman who gave birth to a limb, once the limb emerged and returned. For she too renders impure going forward, and therefore the law of one who has relations with her is the same as that of one who has relations with a woman who saw a stain once it was found (see the explanation above halakhah 8).
four women, their present time suffices. They render impure only from the moment they saw, since they are presumed not to see blood (see also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 9:4-5).
once her pregnancy is recognizable. That the pregnancy is noticeable, which is three months from its beginning (ibid.).
she aborted wind. A condition in which a woman's body goes through a false pregnancy process, at the end of which it turns out that there was never a fetus in the womb at all.
or something that is not a fetus. Because of which she does not become impure with the impurity of childbirth (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:8-11).

she remains in her presumption, and her present time suffices. The blood she saw before does not render impure retroactively, since for this purpose she is treated as a pregnant woman, who does not normally see blood.
she becomes retroactively impure like all women. Since at the time she saw it she was not presumed pregnant, the blood she saw renders impure retroactively.
even if her son died etc.. For the absence of menstrual blood depends not on nursing but on the birth itself.
any woman who has never seen blood in her life. Who has not yet ever seen niddah blood.
they said 'a virgin of blood'. Since her menstrual cycle has not yet begun, she is called a virgin.
and she does not mind. She is not angry.
three periods. Ninety days (since an average period of a cycle is thirty days; Commentary to the Mishnah, Niddah 1:5, based on Bavli Niddah 9b).
she is like all women and renders impure retroactively. For now it has become clear that her cycle did not stop but only lengthened.
flowing for all seven. Seeing blood continuously all seven days of niddah.
dripping. Drop after drop.
this counts as one time. And she is still considered a virgin whose present time suffices.

this counts as two times. And from the second or third time that a virgin sees blood she ceases to be considered a virgin and begins to render impure retroactively like other women (as explained below halakhot 3-4).
a girl whose time to see has not come. Who is a minor (not yet twelve years and a day).

three months passed over her and afterward she saw, her present time suffices etc.. Although she already saw three times and was established as seeing blood, since she did not see again for three months she returns to the law of a girl, and renders impure retroactively only after three new times.
another three months and she saw, she renders impure retroactively. As above halakhah 1 regarding an old woman.
the second time she renders impure retroactively. For since her time to see has come, she renders impure retroactively already from the second time.

three months passed over her and afterward she saw, her present time suffices. Although a girl whose time to see has come becomes retroactively impure already the second time, she does not become established as seeing blood until she sees three times, and therefore if she did not see for three months she returns to her prior status of her present time sufficing (Or Sameach below halakhah 5 and others).
as we have explained. Above 3:4.

and if they saw the first time through duress, even the second time their present time suffices. Although a sighting through duress also renders a woman impure (above 1:2, Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 5:1), it does not cause the woman to become retroactively impure because of it.
and three months passed over her and afterward she saw, her present time suffices. For since they did not see for three months they returned to their former status.

one who sees blood after the blood of purity within twenty-four hours. A woman who gave birth and saw blood in the day after forty days from the birth of a male or eighty days from the birth of a female (before which day her blood was pure; see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 4:5).

her present time suffices. Since until now she was presumed not to see impure blood (for example, if she already saw once since the birth, in which case her present time does not suffice by the law of a nursing woman as above halakhah 5; see Aruch LaNer, Niddah 36a).
and every woman who checks frequently is praiseworthy etc.. See also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 8:11.
for the examination is of no use to them. For the niddah is already impure in any case, and a woman sitting on blood of purity is pure even if she sees blood.
because of the pure foods of the evening. To determine whether the pure foods the woman handled last night after the previous examination are pure or retroactively impure.
and every woman who eats terumah examines herself etc.. A woman permitted to eat terumah must check whether she became impure, since terumah is eaten only in purity (Hilchot Terumot 6:1-2).

when she is about to have marital relations because of the pure foods. Since she must in any case examine herself twice a day for the pure foods, they also required her to examine herself before marital relations to permit her to her husband (Bavli Niddah 11b).
who have a regular cycle. A fixed periodicity (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 8:1-10).

in a presumption of purity for their husbands. They need not worry that they saw and became forbidden to their husbands as a niddah (and regarding women who have no regular cycle see there 4:16 and Piskim veShitot there).
as we have explained regarding niddah. There 4:9.
before they reached their time. Whose time to see has not yet come.
and women do not examine them. Adult women experienced in seeing do not need to examine the minors to see if they became impure.

they require examination and women examine them. And they do not examine themselves, since they are not yet accustomed to seeing they do not know how to examine properly and their examination cannot be relied on.
the deaf-mute woman, the imbecile woman etc.. Who cannot examine themselves (and see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 8:15 regarding a blind woman).

all stains that come from among Israel are presumed impure, and those from among gentiles are pure. Blood stains of Jewish women render impure on the presumption that they are niddah blood. But blood stains of gentile women are pure, since gentiles are impure as niddot only by rabbinic law, and the Sages did not decree impurity on their stains (Commentary to the Mishnah 7:3).
except those found in holes and around the privies. For it is likely that they hid them there because they are impure.

and the impurity of all of them is in doubt, as we have explained. For only blood coming from the womb is impure, but a blood stain that we do not know for certain came from there renders impure only out of doubt (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 9:2).

one passes seven cleansing agents over them. Seven specific cleaning substances used to test whether it is blood or dye (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 9:37-38), and also for washing out the stain and nullifying it (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 8:10, Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 12:5).
he immerses it. The garment in which the impure stain was found.
and prepares pure foods upon it. He uses it for pure foods, since it is no longer impure.
and nullifies it. Thereby the stain no longer renders impure, and afterward he immerses the garment to purify it.

if it was fresh he tests it with a needle. He sticks a needle into the surface of the garment, since semen hardens and the needle feels it (for example, where the semen has not dried completely, for if it has it does not render impure; Eizehu Mekoman, Niddah 61b; or because semen itself always remains impure even when dried, but does not render others impure; Tosafot Rid there).

and if it was ground, he tests it in the sun. He holds it against the sun, since semen is opaque and the sun's rays do not penetrate it (and in a new garment this cannot be done, since it is stiff and thick and cannot be examined well in the sun).
its appearance. Its color.

and the pure foods are impure, for he showed that he is particular about the stain, to remove it. Since after the immersion he passed the seven agents over the stain, he revealed that he is particular about it, and therefore the first immersion did not help purify the garment.
soap. Soap.
even though soap removes the dye. And therefore we do not know now whether it was a stain or dye.
and passed them again a second time and it came off. Since the stain came off through the agents, there is concern that it was blood that for some reason did not come off in the first examination.

and all the pure foods prepared on it after the second washing are impure, since he showed that he is particular about it etc.. Since he passed agents over it again he revealed that he is now particular about the stain, and therefore pure foods prepared from now on will be impure.
we have already explained in Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah. 9:37-38.
it renders impure as a stain, like menstrual blood. That is, this blood is regarded as menstrual blood and renders impure like it.
for the source is impure in its place. See also above 1:9.
even though the blood came out after she died etc.. Since the woman died, this blood cannot be defined as menstrual blood, but since it came from the impure womb it renders impure as a stain.

and if it contained a revi'it, it renders impure in a tent. Like the law of a revi'it of blood from a corpse (Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:12; but corpse blood without a revi'it does not render impure, there 3:15).

and it renders impure as a stain. For we are stringent with this blood, treating it both as corpse blood, which renders impure in a tent, and as niddah blood, which renders impure in any amount (above 1:8).
they always remain in their impurity etc.. See also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 4:3.
until they immerse. Immersion in a mikveh as required (see there 11:16).
without seeing impurity. Without seeing blood or discharge that renders them impure.
after seven for a male and fourteen for a female. After seven days from the birth of a male or fourteen from the birth of a female.

even though it is within the days of purity. Within thirty-three days for a male or sixty-six for a female. During these days the law of a woman who gave birth is that any blood she sees is called 'blood of purity' and does not render her impure (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 4:5).
and it renders impure when moist and dry. As above 2:1.
Scripture did not make it depend on days alone, but on days and immersion. The purity of a woman who gave birth does not depend only on a fixed number of days passing, but also on her immersing.
who went down to immerse from impurity to purity. To pass from the days of impurity to the days of purity.
and it came out between the teeth. Outside the cervix, in which case the woman becomes impure as a niddah (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 5:2).
she is impure. Although the woman was purified of the impurity of childbirth, she becomes impure because of the blood that was dislodged from her and was not purified by the immersion.

even though it is still in her flesh. Although the blood has not yet left her body, since it left the womb before the immersion of the woman who gave birth, it is considered niddah blood that renders impure and not blood of purity.

or after counting seven clean days, if she gave birth with a discharge. A woman who saw blood during the days of her discharge before the birth, not because of the fetus, is called one who gave birth with a discharge, and must count seven days clean of blood and only afterward may immerse and begin her days of purity (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 7:1-8).

like an impure person who immersed and the sun has not yet set etc.. Like a person who became impure with a primary source of impurity and immersed, and the evening after his immersion has not yet come, who is a second-degree impurity (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 10:1).

but with respect to sacred things she is like a first-degree impurity, since she has not yet immersed. And she renders impure the sacred things she touches and makes them second-degree impure (unlike a tevul yom, who only disqualifies sacred things and makes them fourth-degree impure; see there 5:3).
but like one who touched a niddah or a corpse-impure person and the like. Who are primary sources of impurity, and one who touches them becomes first-degree impure.
she may eat from the tithe. She is permitted to eat second tithe (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:4).
and she disqualifies terumah like a tevul yom, as will be explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 10:3.
and from her blood of purity. The blood she sees in these days, which is blood of purity.
for the liquid of a tevul yom is pure, as will be explained. There 5:4, and see also halakhah 6 there.

and she renders sacred things impure like a derivative of impurities until she completes the days of purity and is pure for everything, and it seems to me... that she needs immersion at the end and afterward she may touch sacred things. From the language here it appears that a woman who gave birth whose days of purity are completed does not render sacred things impure by touch, but that they required her to immerse before touching sacred things since during the days of purity she rendered them impure as a first-degree impurity. And although as long as she has not brought her offering she lacks atonement and is forbidden to eat sacred things, nevertheless she does not render them impure by touch. So the Rambam held at first, but afterward he retracted this view and held that one lacking atonement disqualifies sacred things by touch like a tevul yom (see Rabbi Yosef Kafih's note to the Commentary to the Mishnah, Zevachim 12a and Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 10:3 and the explanation there; accordingly it seems that what is said here is from the text of the first edition of the Rambam). Some explained the halakhah here according to the Rambam's view after he retracted, and explained that this speaks of a woman who gave birth who has brought her offering, and nevertheless they required her to immerse before she touches sacred things. Although the Sages required those lacking atonement to immerse after bringing their offering to permit them to eat sacred things, they did not require immersion for touching (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 12:15); that is for other people lacking atonement, but for a woman who gave birth they were more stringent and required immersion for touching too (see Merkevet HaMishneh).

her blood of purity is impure like her saliva and her urine. Although this blood is blood of purity, it is impure by the law of the liquids of the metzora, which are impure (and it renders impure like them only when moist, and not like other impure blood, which renders impure even when dry, as explained above 2:1).
for all impure persons, the liquids that come out of them are like the liquids they touch. That they are first-degree impure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 10:4).
three liquids that come out of him. His saliva, his semen, and his urine.
as we have explained. Above 1:14-15.
a minor zavah. Who saw blood one or two days and must now keep one clean day in order to become pure.
after sunrise. After the sun has risen.
as we have explained regarding the prohibition of a niddah. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:9.
her touch and her relations are in suspension. Their status is in doubt, until it becomes clear at the end of the day of observation whether she saw or not (see also there halakhot 13-14).
and exempt. From a sin offering.
and if she saw blood after she immersed. It turns out that she was a zavah that entire day that passed and renders impure retroactively.
and one who has relations with her is liable for a sin offering. As one who unwittingly had relations with a zavah, who is liable for an offering.

before dawn rose, it is as if she had not immersed. See also there halakhah 12. But if she immersed after dawn rose, even though sunrise had not yet come, her immersion is valid after the fact (Mishnah Megillah 2:4).

one who sees blood on the eleventh day. Which is the last day of the days of discharge, since the next day the days of niddah begin (for the details of the cycle of niddah days and zivah days see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:2-6).

she renders impure by lying and sitting, even though she is not fit to be a major zavah. For immersion on the night of observation is not considered immersion, as above. And although even if she sees on the twelfth day she will not become a major zavah (for then the days of niddah begin and do not combine with the sightings of the days of zivah), nevertheless she is considered a minor zavah who renders impure by lying and sitting (though the immersion at night helps in that if her husband had relations with her they are exempt from an offering; there halakhah 17).
as we have explained regarding the prohibition of a niddah. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:17.
even though she is forbidden to have relations until evening. Like the law of every minor zavah, who is forbidden to her husband all day of observation (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:18).
as we have explained there regarding the prohibition of a niddah. There.
therefore she need not observe the twelfth day etc.. Since the days of zivah were completed she left the status of zavah, and her immersion purifies her for purposes of pure foods.
even though she is not fit to be a major zavah. For she becomes a major zavah only when she sees three consecutive days within the days of zivah.
as we have explained there regarding niddah. There halakhah 16.
who immersed on their seventh day. For the zav and the major zavah count seven clean days and immerse on the seventh day and are pure by evening.
as we have explained. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:11, Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 3:1.

and they void the seven days of counting. Even if they saw on the seventh day after they immersed they must count anew and render impure retroactively (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:13-15, Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah there; and see also Hilchot Tum'at Okhelin 8:19).

they do not render earthenware vessels impure by moving after they immersed. For the zav and his like who moved an earthenware vessel render it impure even when sealed with a tight lid (below 8:2-3). Since this is an extra impurity of the zav that other impure persons do not have, it is remedied by this immersion (Rashi, Megillah 8b, cited in Kesef Mishneh, and see there another reason).
we have already explained. Above 1:1.

for the lying place fit for lying and the seat fit for sitting. The 'lying place' stated in the Torah includes the vessels fit for lying, and the 'seat' includes all those fit for sitting, which the zav renders impure.

and whether he sat on a lying place or lay on a seat, he rendered it impure. Although the lying place is used for lying and the seat for sitting, if the impure person sat on the lying place or lay on the seat he rendered it impure.
the saddle cloth of a donkey and the saddle of a horse. Types of saddle fit for riding (see further examples of vessels impure through riding in Hilchot Kelim 25:20).
before he separated from the things that render him impure. While he is still touching the lying place that renders him impure.

each of these is a primary source of impurity, and a person who touched one of them or carried them renders garments impure etc.. And the same applies to every primary source of impurity that renders impure by touch and carrying, that it renders garments impure at the time of touching or carrying, except the riding vessel and the carcass, which do not render garments impure at the time of touching (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 6:12).
you have learned that every impure person of whom it is said 'he shall wash his clothes' etc.. See also Hilchot Parah 5:2.
that does not render garments impure because it is a derivative. For a derivative of impurity renders impure only food and drink (Hilchot Tum'at Met 5:7).
as we have explained. In the previous paragraphs.
that are carried above the zav. Even many vessels placed one on top of the other that do not touch him (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Zavim 4:6, Hilchot Tum'at Met 5:14).

they are called madaf. In the sense of 'nadaf' (driven), that the impurity spreads like a scent that wafts afar. For the zav renders impure all the vessels above him even when there are many partitions between them (Commentary to the Mishnah there).
and the metzora. Who also renders lying places and seats impure (Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 10:11).
that it rot. That it decay.
as we have explained. Above 2:10.
or the lying place that is above. The one adjacent to the stone beneath it.
if it touched it at the time of his lying. If each lying place touched the next while the zav lay on top of them.
all are impure and first-degree impure. By the law of madaf impurity (above halakhah 3), which applies to anything carried above the zav.

except for the person who is on top of the zav... he renders other vessels impure, as we have explained. For a person carried on top of the zav renders impure garments and vessels that he touches while on the zav, just as a person who touches the zav renders garments impure as long as he has not separated from him, as explained above halakhah 2.
like anyone who carries something that renders impure by carrying. As explained in Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:6.
for the carrier is first-degree impure. And only a person becomes impure through the impurity of carrying, not vessels (there halakhah 9).

except that the person is first-degree, and vessels made for lying... are primary sources of impurity, as we have explained. Above halakhah 5 (regarding vessels), and the beginning of this halakhah (regarding a person).
suspended. That the zav became suspended by it, such as by a scale pan (see below 8:6, Commentary to the Mishnah, Zavim 4:5).
even if it was under the stone. As above 6:5.

and this person who is above the madras renders garments impure as long as he has not separated from the things that render him impure, as we have explained. For the law of a person who is above the madras is the same as the law of one who touches it, that he renders garments impure as long as he has not separated from the things that render him impure (above 6:2).
since he did not touch, it is pure. For had he touched, it would have become impure even by touch of only part of it (Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:3-4).
the entire lying place and the entire riding vessel become impure. For with respect to the lying place and riding vessel themselves there is no distinction between part of them and all of them.

placed lengthwise they are impure... placed widthwise they are pure. When the zav lies along the length of the benches, most of him is likely to be on each of them separately, and therefore he renders them impure, unlike when he lies across their width (Rashi, Shabbat 93a, Rosh and Rash, Zavim 4:4). In the Commentary to the Mishnah (there) the Rambam explained the opposite, that when the zav's length is across the width of the benches they are impure because he lies on all of them, unlike when he lies along their length (and see Chazon Nachum there, that the Rambam here retracted what he wrote there).

both are impure. Since the zav is likely to rest most of his weight on each leg separately (Kiryat Sefer), or because even half of the zav's body is considered most of him for this purpose (Aruch HaShulchan 115:16).
because it cannot stand on three. Since with one leg missing the bed would fall, each leg is considered as bearing most of the zav.
and one who assists is nothing. The assistant is not considered one of the bearers since it can be carried without him.

for impurity was not established in any one of them etc.. Since the four legs of the animal bear the zav equally, there is no presumption of impurity in one more than another, and therefore all are pure.
if one lying place was placed under the two forelegs of the animal etc.. That the lying place is long so that two of the animal's forelegs or legs are on the same lying place.

the impure person sat on the beam of an olive press etc.. The beam of the olive press rests on the akal (a kind of round basket made of ropes) and serves to press the olives within it to produce oil. Therefore when the zav sits on the beam, all the vessels in the akal are impure since they bear his weight.
a launderer's press. Which has two boards made to press and flatten the garments placed between them.

because it is loose and the press's support rests on its legs. For the upper board of the press does not rest on the garments but on the legs of the press, and therefore the zav sitting on it does not render the garments impure (see Tosafot Yom Tov, Zavim 4:7, Merkevet HaMishneh).

for if one wishes to insert... he can insert even though it is tied. Even when the press is closed and the boards are tightened to each other, the upper board does not rest on the garments, since even then one can insert a knife or other thin utensil between the boards (the exact reality of the press discussed here is not entirely clear; see Commentary to the Mishnah, Zavim there, and the Raavad).
that was not made for lying... even though it is fit for lying. That was not made for lying or sitting although it can be used for that.
for they say to him. To the person sitting on this vessel.
stand up, and we will do our work with this vessel. For this vessel is not meant for sitting but for work.
he turned over a se'ah measure and sat on it, turned over a trough etc.. Large vessels used for measuring or kneading and the like, which he turned upside down and sat upon.
the sail of a ship. The ship's sail.

as it says: on which he sits, that which is designated for sitting. From the grammatical form 'yeshev' in the extended present tense (and not 'yashav' in the past tense) it implies that this refers to a vessel the zav is accustomed to sit on.
if the vessel serves for sitting along with the work for which it was made. That in addition to its use for its work it is also used for sitting.
the radid. A garment covering the whole body.
and the turmel and the chemet. Leather bags large enough to sit on (Hilchot Kelim 24:11, 27:10 specify the size that makes them susceptible to madras impurity).
and in Hilchot Kelim. Chapters 22-27.
we already explained at the beginning of this book. Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:7.
a beam was resting on top of a fence. So that the middle of the beam rests on the thickness of the fence and its two sides are on the two sides of the fence.

even earthenware vessels... it is as if he touched them and rendered them impure. Although an earthenware vessel does not become impure through touch on its outer side, it becomes impure through the zav's moving it. For one who moves is like one who touches the entire vessel, and therefore it is considered as if the zav touched the vessel from inside (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 6:3).
needless to say if the zav carried the person etc.. Since the zav renders impure through a slight movement alone as moving, all the more so he renders impure by actual carrying.

an earthenware vessel sealed with a tight lid. That has a close and tightened cover that saves it from becoming impure in a tent of the dead (Hilchot Tum'at Met 21:1), and since its opening is closed the zav cannot touch it from inside and render it impure, yet he renders it impure by moving, which is considered as if he touched it from inside.
hollow like a ball and no mouth has yet been made for it. That is hollow inside and no opening has yet been made.
like the lepasin arniyot. A kind of bowls (alfasim) that when made are formed as a hollow ball that is divided in two after it dries.

into the airspace of an earthenware vessel... it is pure. Although an earthenware vessel into whose airspace impurity entered becomes impure even if the impurity does not touch it from inside (Hilchot Tum'at Met 6:3).

for a niddah and her like do not render impure by limbs. And since only one limb of the impure person entered the airspace of the earthenware vessel, he does not render it impure (and see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 6:3, that this sentence has an additional meaning).
a cane held in his folds. That he held a stick in the creased places of his body, such as the armpit.

for one who moves impurity is like one who carries it. That a pure person's moving the zav has the same law as every moving in all impurities, that it is like carrying (above halakhah 1, Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:7).
as we have explained at the beginning of this book. Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:8.
the zav lowered. The pan in which the zav was went down and the second pan, in which the vessel was, went up.
they are like vessels that he touched. That they are first-degree impure.

for they carried the zav, as if he stood on them. For it is considered that the zav was suspended on the lying place, and this is one of the ways in which the zav renders the lying place impure to make it a primary source of impurity (above 7:1, Commentary to the Mishnah, Zavim 4:5).
other vessels. That are not used for lying or riding.

whether they went down or the zav went down, all are first-degree impure. When the zav went down he moved them and it is as if he touched them, and makes them first-degree impure. And when they went down: in the case of a person, he moved the zav and became impure as one who carries a zav. And in the case of other vessels or food and drink, although they ordinarily do not become impure when they carry impurity (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:9), in this case, since had the zav not been in the scale pan the vessels and food in the other pan would have gone down to the ground, whereas now they are raised slightly above the ground, it turns out that the zav carries them and they become impure (Rash and Rosh, Zavim 4:6).
when they wobble. That the bench or board is not fixed in its place but moves.
on a tree whose strength is poor. That sways when people climb on it.
for the thickness of its trunk is not enough to carve out a quarter of a kav. For its trunk is not wide enough to carve in it a receptacle of a quarter of a kav.

on a branch. Most commentators explained that this means a branch (from the language 'and he cut down a branch of trees', Judges 9:48; see the commentators on the Mishnah, Zavim 3:1, Bavli Bava Metzia 105b), but some explained that the Rambam here means a sukkah like the festival sukkah (see Radbaz, Rabbi Yosef Kafih), and accordingly it should be vocalized here 'besukkah'.
and that is when the one hiding in it and pressing it makes it move. That the person hiding on it presses it and moves it (Radbaz, and see other explanations in the commentators on the Bavli there).
on an Egyptian ladder. Which is small.
that cannot tilt under a person. That does not lean and sway when a person climbs it.
even if they climbed from one side. For in this way they put more weight on one side and it is possible that they would move one another.
one closing and one opening, it became impure. For in such a case they move each other.
as we have explained. Above halakhah 2.
they stretch with ropes. They stretch the wool or flax threads to make ropes from them.
this one pulls going and that one pulls going. Each one pulls the rope toward himself.
whether standing or sitting. Whether with looms standing on the ground or with those that sit on the ground.
when their load is heavy it is impure. For in a case where the load loaded on or unloaded from the donkey is heavy, the zav leans on the pure person because of the weight of the load.
it is pure. For here there is no concern about moving (for example, if he strikes him with a stick or the like without touching him; Chazon Ish, Zavim 4:1).

and therefore even the pure person's garments are impure. And they are a primary source of impurity, like vessels fit for lying on which the zav leaned (above 7:1; Tiferet Yisrael, Zavim 3:3, Aruch HaShulchan 117:11).
became impure. Although with respect to the impurity of a lying place only most of a zav renders impure (as above 7:3), this is not so for a person who carries the zav or is carried by him.
the zav's attachments. Things attached to his body.
these are pure. For since the thing on which the vessels or foods lie is firmly attached, the vessels on it were not moved as a direct result of the blow but were affected by it indirectly.
a tree or a branch of poor strength, or on an Egyptian ladder. See above 8:7.
the bolt. The bar of the door.
the oar. Of the ship.
these are impure. For these things shake when struck.
the beam. A large beam.
these are pure. For these things are stable.
even if it was terumah. For we are stricter with it than with unconsecrated food in a case of doubt about the zav's moving (see Mishnah Zavim 3:2 and Rash and Rosh there).
it is pure. For the oven is among the stable things.

and if a shard from the oven was stuck to the loaf that fell... it is impure. Since the loaf was stuck to the oven so firmly that a piece of the oven was torn off with the loaf, it certainly fell from the force of the blow.
a lying place or riding vessel renders vessels or foods and drinks impure only by touch. Unlike a person, whom the lying place renders impure in seven ways (above 7:2).

but if the vessels or foods and drinks were above the madras... they are pure. Unlike the zav himself, who when they are above him renders them impure with madaf impurity even if he does not touch them (above 6:3).
that can tilt under one person. That tilts when only one person climbs it.
on a raft. A raft.

even though their garments do not touch one another... lest the zav leaned on them. For it is possible that the zav was suspended on these garments or leaned on them even though he did not touch them directly, and in these cases they become a primary source of impurity (above 7:1).
except for the kupach on her head. The kerchief on her head.
and likewise the garments on top of the mast of the ship. Garments hanging at the top of the mast of the ship in which the zav is sitting.
pure. For there is no concern that the impure person leaned on them.
one squeezed at a mill etc.. A pure person standing in a cramped place by the mill while the impure person grinds in it (Chazon Ish, Taharot 7:12).
for the gentile is among them. For gentiles render impure like zavim by rabbinic law (above 2:10).

he is presumed impure and his garments are madras for pure foods. The Sages regarded him as impure like a zav with respect to pure foods, and his garments as impure with madras impurity that renders pure foods impure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 13:1).
and if he touched an earthenware vessel from its airspace. On its inner side, for an earthenware vessel does not become impure through touch on its back (Hilchot Tum'at Met 6:3, Hilchot Kelim 13:1).
even though their impurity is in doubt. For they are among the six doubts for which terumah is burned even though their impurity is rabbinic (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 13:13).

and he should be careful with washing the hands and the purity of the hands. For they decreed that all hands are second-degree impure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 8:8), and therefore they require washing to purify them (see Hilchot Mikva'ot, chapter 11).
and that he not take moist food from an am ha'aretz. Moist foods that were made susceptible to impurity, which, being in the possession of the am ha'aretz, are presumed impure.
and that he not host him in his garment. The chaver should not host an am ha'aretz while the latter is wearing his garment, since his clothes are madras for pure foods.
who behaves modestly inside his house. Who is careful about pure foods even when he is at home, not only for appearance.
and we accept him first regarding the purity of the hands. To rely on him that he washes his hands, so that if he touched pure foods they did not become impure.
and afterward we accept him regarding pure foods. To be trusted about them (Rashi, Bekhorot 30b).
and if he said, I accept only the purity of the hands, we accept him. For this matter alone.

even for pure foods we do not accept him. Since he did not accept upon himself the purity of the hands, which is a light matter, we do not rely on him to accept the other things (Rashi there). Or because the purity of the hands is a basic condition for observing pure foods (Kesef Mishneh).
we suspect him for thirty days. We do not rely on him as a chaver until this length of time passes from the time of his acceptance.
distinction. Distinction.
an elder who sits in the academy. Who was ordained as a sage and judges with the sages.
he need not accept. Even after the destruction (Meiri Arukh).
the wife of a chaver, his sons, the members of his household, and his servants are like the chaver. See also Hilchot Ma'aser 10:2 regarding reliability about tithes.
the wife of an am ha'aretz or his daughter etc.. See also Hilchot Ma'aser 10:3 regarding reliability about tithes.
if others handled them they are forbidden as they were before. For he is not trusted about pure foods that other amei ha'aretz handled when he himself was still an am ha'aretz.
these are permitted to him and forbidden to everyone. For although he is trusted regarding himself, he is not trusted regarding others since at that time he was an am ha'aretz.
and the chaver is asked about his pure foods etc.. The chaver is trusted to rule that his pure foods are pure if a question arose about them.
a chaver who became a king's tax collector or a customs collector and the like. These people collect taxes for the king in various ways.

they remove him from his status as chaver. For those who engage in these roles may be suspected of robbery, since at times they take money for themselves without permission (see Hilchot Gezelah 5:11, Hilchot Edut 10:4).
and he became suspect about one matter. That they saw he is not careful about one of the things that chaverim are careful about.
until it is known that he has repented fully. That he has turned from his deeds completely and it is clear that he is not acting deceitfully (for examples see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 8:9).
the Sabbatical year produce. Produce of the Sabbatical year, which it is forbidden by the Torah to damage or to trade in, and which is subject to removal (see Hilchot Shemittah, chapters 5-7).
he is suspect regarding pure foods. Suspected of selling impure foods on the presumption that they are pure (see Hilchot Shemittah 8:16).
as will be explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 7:1.

he is believed to testify with it for others and to judge with it for others. He is permitted to testify to the fitness of others or to judge their matters, although he himself sins in the matter under discussion (see also Hilchot Shemittah 8:17).
it is a presumption that a person does not sin so that others may benefit. We assume that a person will not lie and cause people to stumble for another person's benefit (see Hilchot Ma'aser 12:17).
we have already explained. Hilchot Parah 13:12.

they are believed about the purity of the sin-offering cow. If they said of something that it is pure for the sanctification of the red heifer's ashes water or its sprinkling, they are believed, although this level of purity is stricter than that of sacred things and terumah (as detailed in chapter 13 there).
about the purity of wine and oil of libations. Wine and oil that were consecrated for libations and meal offerings.
at the time of the winepresses and the olive presses. At the time when grapes are trodden in the winepress and olives in the olive press to make wine and oil.
he should not accept it from him. As pure terumah, but he may accept it on the understanding that it is doubtfully disqualified (Commentary to the Mishnah, Chagigah 3:4).
last year. The past year.
and immerses him. The am ha'aretz, who is presumed impure.
that are not susceptible. That were not wetted by liquids that make foods susceptible to impurity (see Hilchot Tum'at Okhelin 1:1-2).
with sacred wine or oil inside it. Inside the jar there is wine or oil of sacred status for libations.
since he is believed about the purity of sacred things. As above halakhah 1.
he is believed about the purity of the vessel. Although he has not yet consecrated the libations, he is believed to keep the vessel pure for that purpose.

but before seventy they are not believed. Although amei ha'aretz are believed about the purity of wine and oil of libations all year (above halakhah 1), and the same applies to vessels full of them (as implied above halakhah 4), this is only for libations already consecrated (Radbaz, and see Commentary to the Mishnah, Chagigah 3:4).
about an earthenware vessel. Which has no purification in a mikveh (see Hilchot Mikva'ot 1:3).

even though the liquids inside it are impure. For the liquids of an am ha'aretz are presumed impure. And although impure liquids render vessels impure by rabbinic law (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 7:1-3), here they did not decree this impurity (see Bavli Chagigah 26a).
his garment, which is madras. As above 10:1.

because kilns are not made in Jerusalem. For the Sages enacted that kilns (in which earthenware vessels are produced) not be made in Jerusalem because of the smoke (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:14). And because earthenware vessels were less available in Jerusalem, the Sages eased their impurity, and the amei ha'aretz themselves were more careful not to make them impure (Commentary to the Mishnah, Chagigah 3:6).

from Modi'it inward. The area from the city of Modi'in to Jerusalem (about 15 kilometers; and likewise this distance in every direction, Piskei Rid, Chagigah 25b). For the boundary up to Modi'in is considered adjacent to the Temple and serves Temple needs, and beyond this distance is considered a 'distant road' from Jerusalem (Mishnah Pesachim 9:2).
a chaver was entering and an am ha'aretz was leaving. The chaver is on his way to Jerusalem and the am ha'aretz on his way back from it, and they met at Modi'in.
he is believed at Modi'it to say that it is pure for sacred things. And the chaver can buy the vessel from him there.

if both were entering or both were leaving he is not believed until he is inside Modi'it. Since both are on the same road, the chaver can take the earthenware vessel from the am ha'aretz inside Modi'in, and therefore he is not believed at Modi'in itself (Rashi, Chagigah 25b, cited in Kesef Mishneh).
and he took the pot and entered with it, it is pure for sacred things. Even when the buyer is an am ha'aretz.
as we have explained. Above halakhot 5-6.

he took a pot and left with it outside Modi'it, it is impure both for terumah and for sacred things. This applies only when the buyer is an am ha'aretz; but if the buyer is a chaver, the pot remains in its purity even outside Modi'it (Rabbi Yosef Kafih).

these are pure. For even when the potter is an am ha'aretz the vessel becomes impure through him only after its firing in the kiln, and as long as it is in the kiln no person has touched it and it is pure (Commentary to the Mishnah, Parah 5:1).
even if he took from the first row. From the outer row of vessels arranged inside the kiln, which is closest to the opening, and the concern that an am ha'aretz touched it is greater.
and half of it was already taken. Half of the vessels inside it were already taken.
on the festival. During the three pilgrimage festivals.
for all Israel are chaverim on the festival. See also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 13:8.
because everyone purifies himself etc.. For all Israel are commanded to be pure on the festival so that they can enter the Temple and eat sacred food (Hilchot Tum'at Okhelin 16:10).
on the table. The table of the showbread.
and it turns out he needs immersion and the setting of the sun. Like a tevul yom, who becomes completely pure only after he has immersed and waited for evening.

and it is said of the showbread, before Me always. Since the showbread must always be on the table, they took care not to cause the table impurity, so that it would not require immersion and they would have to remove the bread from it.

because their plating is as if nullified relative to them. For although they are plated with gold and copper, which are materials that become impure, this plating is nullified relative to the altars themselves, which do not become impure (Bavli Chagigah 27a).
and he does not need sprinkling. There is no need to sprinkle red heifer ashes water on him, since he is trusted that he is pure from corpse impurity.
and one sprinkles on him on the third and seventh. On the third and seventh day of his purification (see Hilchot Parah 11:1-2).
like all vessels found anywhere outside Jerusalem. Which are presumed impure, lest they became impure through a zav or a corpse.
as will be explained in the impurity of doubts. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 13:4-5.
if he knows he eats terumah. If the am ha'aretz knows that the chaver who deposited with him eats terumah, in which case he is careful not to make his vessels impure.
pure from corpse impurity. For an am ha'aretz is believed to say of a vessel that it is pure from corpse impurity (above 11:12).
and pure from corpse impurity. Since they are not entirely in the am ha'aretz's possession, they have only madras impurity.

he put them on his shoulder etc.. In which case they are entirely in his possession (Radbaz cited in Kesef Mishneh). Some explain that in the first clause, where he does not move the vessels from their place, we rely on him to guard them from corpse impurity, but when he puts them on his shoulder and takes them with him, we worry that he will not know to be careful not to pass under a tent of impurity and the like (Rash, Taharot 7:7, Chazon Ish there 8:9).
and we teach him not to do so. Not to leave his vessels in public places.
he left his winepress and pit. Filled with wine.
in the niches. Compartments.
even if he found the seal damaged, his vessels are pure. For we attribute it to the seal having been damaged by itself (Chazon Ish, Taharot 8:7; and see also Hilchot Tum'at Okhelin 11:16).
that is not sealed with a tight lid. That does not have a close and tightened cover, so that it becomes impure easily through touch from its airspace (see above 10:1).

the foods, drinks, and earthenware vessel... are impure. For these things have a light impurity, in that they never become primary sources of impurity (Hilchot Tum'at Met 5:6, Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 10:8-9), and therefore they decreed impurity on them when an am ha'aretz guards them, even though the homeowner watches from afar (Commentary to the Mishnah, Taharot 7:5).

and an earthenware vessel sealed with a tight lid. Which becomes impure only through the zav's carrying (above 8:3, Hilchot Tum'at Met 6:3), and therefore they did not decree impurity on it in this case.
even if he was bound or his hands and feet were cut off. So that he cannot walk and make the contents of the house impure.
and left him awake and found him awake... everything in the house is pure. For the am ha'aretz fears touching things in the house lest the homeowner come and see him.

he left him asleep and found him awake... impure. For in this case we worry that he stretched out his hand to see the things in the house since he had not seen them before (Commentary to the Mishnah, Taharot 7:2)

,. Some explained that in this case the am ha'aretz is not worried that the homeowner will come soon, since having left him asleep he supposes that he is still asleep (Aruch HaShulchan and Mishnah Rishonah, Taharot 7:2).
even if the mill stopped. She finished grinding at the mill and now has time to touch the household vessels.
and even if there were two. Two women who are amei ha'aretz.
everything in the house is impure. For they search through the whole house and touch everything in it.
because the fear of the gentile is upon them. Because of their fear of the gentile they do not touch things that are not theirs (Commentary to the Mishnah, Taharot 7:6).
in what case is this said. That when they enter alone the whole house is impure.
for the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted. Since we worry about making the house impure only on their word, they are believed to testify that it is pure.
the foods, drinks, and open earthenware vessels. As above halakhah 5.

and if a gentile or a woman is with them, everything is impure. For the gentile renders everything impure like a zav (above 2:10), and a woman is regularly impure as a niddah or zavah (Tosafot Yom Tov, Taharot 7:6), so they decreed impurity on them more than on an am ha'aretz.
out of fear. Fear of being caught.
and they changed their minds. They regretted it.
an axe. An axe.

or an oven sealed with a tight lid, these are impure. Although it is built in and cannot be moved, we worry that the am ha'aretz will remove the tight lid and make the vessel impure (Commentary to the Mishnah, Taharot 8:1).
even though the am ha'aretz can stretch out his hand and touch. Since the chaver's roof is above, the am ha'aretz has no right there at all.

and not because of wine of libation. He does not worry that the gentile will make the wine he places on his roof forbidden, even though the gentile's hand can reach there (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 13:7).

any place where the am ha'aretz can stretch out his hand and touch is presumed impure. Since the am ha'aretz's roof is level with or higher than the chaver's roof, the am ha'aretz may stretch his hand into the chaver's domain, claiming that his belongings rolled there (Kesef Mishneh).
because he is caught as a thief. Since the am ha'aretz has no reason to enter the inner courtyard, he is considered a thief if he puts his hand there without permission.
a courtyard divided by a low partition. A low partition.
his pure foods are pure even though the am ha'aretz's hand reaches. See also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 13:7.
because it was left in the am ha'aretz's domain for one hour. And therefore the bucket is impure, although it is unlikely that the am ha'aretz touched it while it was in the pit.
if his professional tools were in his hand. Tools used for the sale, such as the vessels on which pots are arranged for sale (Meiri, Ketubot 24b).

and if his professional tools are not in his hand, everything is pure; it is presumed that no one touched them. Unlike when he placed them near the public domain, where even if his professional tools are not in his hand the outer ones are impure in any case because of passersby.

a priest who purified his vessels for this winepress and left them for the next winepress. Who purified his vessels used for treading grapes in the winepress, and left them there for the next winepress.
because he eats pure foods. And amei ha'aretz know to be careful not to make his vessels impure (as above 12:1).
unless he says etc.. That he gave thought to guarding these vessels from becoming impure.
he immerses the grape harvesters. For in a harvest made for wine, the Sages decreed that the grapes are susceptible to impurity even if no water fell on them (Hilchot Tum'at Okhelin 11:1).

the oil pressers. The workers who produce oil in the olive press; but the workers who pick the olives from the trees need not be pure, since the olives are not susceptible to impurity until they are ready for pressing in the olive press (see there halakhot 6, 8).
until they are no longer hidden from his eyes. Since they moved so far from him he cannot watch them.
and they wait for sunset. They wait for evening.

and likewise with the children among them. The oil pressers and harvesters are believed to testify that the children did not touch the oil or the olives (Commentary to the Mishnah according to the printed translations and the Ma'or edition; Rabbi Yosef Kafih translated differently).

for amei ha'aretz are not expert in the impurity of moving. They do not know that one who moves is considered as one who carries, and that one who moves a vessel that became impure with madras is impure like one who carries it (Commentary to the Mishnah, Taharot 10:1, and see Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:7).
even though they went more than a mil away. They went farther than a mil (about a kilometer, and compare Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 12:16).
and they say, now he will come, for he is behind us. And he can come quickly by a shortcut without our seeing him (Bavli Chagigah 20b, see Kesef Mishneh).
but if he said to them, go out and I will come after you. From his words it implies that he is not following them, and therefore they are not afraid to touch.
and wrapped in a tallit. Over the robe.
and the magrefah. An iron tool used to scrape the hearth, also used to separate figs stuck together.

and to guard the magrefah from something that makes it impure. To guard that the magrefah not become impure through a primary source of impurity that makes it first-degree impure and capable of rendering others impure.

but not from something that disqualifies it. That it is not guarded from becoming impure through a derivative of impurity that makes it second-degree impure, which disqualifies and renders impure terumah and sacred things (and although by Torah law a vessel does not become impure through a derivative of impurity, it becomes impure by rabbinic law through impure liquids that make it second-degree impure; Tosafot Chagigah 20a; see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 7:2-3; 7:10).
tevul yom. A person who became impure and immersed and the evening after his immersion has not yet come.
for he disqualifies terumah but is pure regarding unconsecrated food. For a tevul yom disqualifies terumah but does not render unconsecrated food impure.
as will be explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 10:1-3.
and if he said, my intention was to guard it even from something that disqualifies it. That he guarded the jar from becoming impure even through a tevul yom.
his Shabbat garments were switched with his weekday garments. So that he wore Shabbat garments instead of weekday garments.

for he does not guard weekday garments like Shabbat garments. For it is customary to guard Shabbat garments more than weekday garments, and since he thinks he is wearing weekday garments, he does not guard the garments as they deserve (Bavli Chagigah 20a).
and they made the vessels impure. Since each of them thinks that the other is the wife of an am ha'aretz, she does not take the trouble to guard her vessels properly (ibid.).
his shawl. A cloth he wraps himself in.
unless he informed him and relied on him. That he asked him to guard his vessels in purity.
he left vessels, they are impure etc.. With vessels they were stricter, since they can be purified (Rash, Taharot 8:1, cited in Kesef Mishneh).

he is not believed. For had he been telling the truth he would have told him the first time, and since he said nothing to him then, there is reason to suspect that he is lying now because he wants to cause him a loss (and see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:15).
